papers.title: Water-Driven Porous Silicon as a Platform for Blue Materials
papers.abstract: Living organisms control water to transport matter, transfer energy and drive chemical reactions. In this perspective, we argue that porous silicon can give engineering materials comparable control over water. Its pore architecture, surface chemistry and semiconducting skeleton can be shaped across length scales with the precision of semiconductor processing and, like the water it can host, it relies on one of the most abundant chemical elements on Earth. Liquids in porous silicon, most often water, can flow as a continuum through pores a few nanometers wide, strain the skeleton through capillary and electrosorption stresses, shift structural color, switch transparency, and modulate or generate electrical signals. We describe three directions to combine and extend these effects and overcome their limitations. Pore hierarchy resolves the classical trade-off between interface area and transport speed by combining large and small pores and thereby allows functions to be scaled from thin planar films to three-dimensional components. Surface modification becomes a design variable that tunes the interaction between water and the pore wall. It can be set locally and, with switchable coatings, on demand. Finally, pores only a few molecules wide alter the properties of water itself. In the absence of a bulk-like volume, water can become dielectrically anisotropic and highly conductive. Altogether, these steps turn porous silicon from a responsive material into an adaptive, water-driven material.

papers.title: Non-local Stabilization and Synchronization of Larmor Precession in Trapped Polariton Condensate Dimer
papers.abstract: We demonstrate mutual synchronization of Larmor precessions between spatially separated, optically trapped polariton condensates. We identify the cross-condensate correlation g(2)1,2({\tau}) as a sensitive metric for condensate coupling. Synchronization of precessions in a condensate dimer is mediated by polariton outflow and resonantly depends on spectral overlap and precession winding. All-optical stirring of one site non-locally increases the pseudo-spin dephasing time of its static neighbor, prolonging phase-locking in a dimer by an order of magnitude. Our work establishes a scalable platform for studying non-equilibrium time-periodically driven systems and for high-speed spinoptronic networks.

papers.title: Proximity Transient Absorption in van der Waals Heterostructures
papers.abstract: Transient absorption spectroscopy is a widely used technique for investigating ultrafast electronic dynamics, where transient optical signals are generally interpreted as arising from excitations within the material hosting the probed optical transition. A distinct form of transient absorption spectroscopy, termed proximity transient absorption (PTA), is demonstrated, in which the probed optical transition and the monitored photoexcited carriers reside in different materials. Using graphene/hBN/WS$_2$ heterostructures, photoexcited carriers in graphene induce a strong transient optical response at the excitonic resonance of a WS$_2$ monolayer through Coulomb screening, even when the two layers remain electronically isolated by an atomically thin hBN spacer. The resulting signal follows the carrier dynamics of graphene rather than those of WS$_2$, demonstrating that the WS$_2$ exciton acts as an optical transducer of electronic processes in a neighboring material. The signal decreases systematically with increasing hBN thickness, confirming its proximity origin while remaining substantial for separations approaching 2 nm. PTA provides a noncontact approach for optically modulating one material using photoexcited carriers in another and enables probing of carrier dynamics in materials that are otherwise difficult to investigate directly. More broadly, PTA establishes a new modality of ultrafast spectroscopy and reveals that transient optical signals in van der Waals heterostructures can originate from excitations residing in spatially separated layers.

papers.title: Boosting fluorescence and polarization with nanophotonics for single-molecule chiral sensing
papers.abstract: Detecting chirality is essential in chemistry and biomedicine. Circular dichroism identifies chiral molecules through their differential absorption of circularly polarized light. However, its sensitivity is limited by vanishing absorption at low concentrations. Fluorescence-based methods have already enabled other optical techniques to reach the single-molecule limit and could, in principle, also extend chiral detection to reach this sensitivity regime. They are marred, however, by the combination of weak fluorescence signals and low polarization contrast. To overcome these limitations, we leverage high-index dielectric nanophotonics to simultaneously enhance both fluorescence and polarization for chiral sensing. We propose a reciprocity-based analytical framework for a chiral dipolar emitter coupled to a nanoantenna and reveal the different contributions and trade-offs governing the enhancement of circularly polarized fluorescence. Guided by this insight, we tailor achiral dielectric nanostructures to reach a 1000-fold enhancement of fluorescence intensity together with a 10-fold increase in polarization. Crucially, we show that accounting for extrinsic polarization effects in the angular emission patterns of nanophotonic structures is indispensable for reliable enantiomer discrimination. Our approach opens a realistic path for single-molecule chiral sensing.

papers.title: Dynamic Hotspot Migration and Self-Induced Resonances in Ultrafast Laser-Irradiated Silicon Thin Films
papers.abstract: The spatial distribution of energy in silicon thin films under femtosecond laser irradiation is demonstrated to be influenced by the interaction between carrier-induced refractive index modulation and self-induced Fabry-P\'erot resonances. We resolve three characteristic excitation regions such as interface-localized, binodal and multi-nodal regimes considering the analysis of silicon-on-insulator (SOI) configurations across thicknesses of 100, 230, and 350 nm. We report a nonlinear hotspot migration effect where the transient reduction of the refractive index stretches the internal standing wave, translating intensity antinodes toward the film volume during the pulse. Numerical results demonstrate that at higher fluences, plasma-induced extinction suppresses internal reflections, triggering a transition from resonance-mediated absorption to plasma shielding. These findings establish a physical basis for depth-resolved modification in laser nanomanufacturing, providing a dual-capacity for simultaneous surface patterning and depth-resolved subsurface modification with direct applications in laser-assisted interfacial separation and 3D integrated photonic fabrication.

papers.title: Optical vortex bullets with large angular momenta
papers.abstract: We investigate three-dimensional spatiotemporal optical vortex solitons (light bullets with a toroidal shape) carrying higher-order orbital angular momentum in Kerr media with anomalous group-velocity dispersion and a transversely localized Gaussian profile of the linear refractive index. Stationary vortex bullets with topological charges (winding numbers) $1\leq \ell \leq 4$ are obtained as numerical solutions of the three-dimensional nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation, and their existence, structure and stability are systematically analyzed. In terms of atomic Bose-Einstein condensates, these solutions represent matter-wave solitons with embedded vorticity. We examine the dependence of the solution families on the propagation constant, the depth and width of the guiding profile, and $\ell $. It is found that the increase of $\ell $ requires one to use a stronger or wider waveguiding potential to sustain localized states satisfying the Vakhitov-Kolokolov (VK) stability criterion. VK-complying and non-complying branches of vortex-soliton families are separated by a degenerate Townes branch. Direct simulations reveal that, although the guiding profile substantially suppresses the collapse and extends the propagation distance of vortex bullets, their robustness is ultimately limited by azimuthal instabilities, whose growth is enhanced for values of $\ell $. These results demonstrate that engineered refractive-index landscapes significantly enlarge the stability domain of spatiotemporal vortex bullets and provide guidelines for supporting optical bullets carrying large orbital angular momenta.

papers.title: Purely equatorial lasing in spherical liquid crystal polymer microlasers with bipolar refractive index profile
papers.abstract: Liquid crystal whispering gallery mode (WGM) microlasers show high sensitivity to external stimuli and distinct spectral features, rendering them ideally suited for various sensing applications. They also offer intrinsic anisotropic optical properties, which can be used to shape and manipulate light even inside spatially highly symmetric structures. Here, we report the fabrication of a spherical bipolar liquid crystal polymer microlaser that tightly confines the optical path of WGMs to the equatorial plane. By controlled anchoring of the liquid crystal mesogens followed by polymerization, a fixed refractive index profile is formed within the spherical microcavity. Consequently, only transverse electric (TE) modes oscillating in the equatorial plane experience the high extraordinary refractive index, allowing to confine lasing into a single plane. Furthermore, we observe a characteristic splitting into sub-modes. By combining hyperspectral imaging, optical modeling, and theoretical calculations, we show that the observed sub-modes originate from the lifting of the energy degeneracy of azimuthal WGMs. The unique ability to confine lasing into a single plane makes these spherical microlasers independent of the exact position of the pump beam, which allows consistent localized sensing especially in combination with fast point scanning microscopes or inside highly dynamic biological environments.

papers.title: Picosecond-resolved entanglement distribution over an urban free-space channel
papers.abstract: Time-evolving entangled states describe quantum particles whose correlations evolve in time according to a well-defined dynamics. Such states can be generated in a variety of physical systems and are promising resources for several quantum technologies, ranging from quantum clock synchronization to quantum communication. However, their full potential is currently limited by the fact that the entanglement dynamics often occur on timescales comparable to the achievable synchronization precision, especially in experiments aimed at distributing entanglement through noisy urban channels. In this context, accurate timing is not merely a technical detail, but a fundamental requirement for faithfully observing and exploiting the underlying quantum correlations. Here, we demonstrate the faithful distribution of a fast-evolving entangled state over a 270 m free-space channel connecting two buildings in the center of Rome. The developed system incorporates a synchronization device capable of achieving sub-50 ps timing accuracy between the two ends of the link while simultaneously supporting channel stabilization. Our results demonstrate that time-evolving entanglement can be reliably transmitted through a noisy urban free-space channel, representing an important benchmark toward long-distance free-space quantum communication and the future implementation of time-correlated entangled states in demanding scenarios such as satellite-based quantum networks.

papers.title: Sideband fingerprints of antibunched light in cascaded quantum wave mixing
papers.abstract: Quantum wave mixing on a single superconducting qubit produces a hierarchy of coherent side peaks associated with elastic multiphoton scattering pathways. In a cascaded source--probe geometry these pathways become sensitive to the photon statistics of the radiation emitted by the source qubit. We develop an analytical theory of this effect starting from the cascaded master equation in the weak-driving regime. In the coherent-filtering limit when the decay rate of the probe qubit is less than that of the source, the standard coherent--coherent wave-mixing hierarchy is recovered. In the opposite limit, side peaks associated with multiphoton absorption from the antibunched source field are parametrically suppressed. Numerical solutions confirm the analytical scaling laws. The resulting sideband hierarchy provides a frequency-domain fingerprint of antibunched itinerant microwave light.

papers.title: Terabit-scale wavelength-multiplexed transmitter enabled by thin-film lithium tantalate
papers.abstract: Artificial-intelligence systems face a growing data-movement bottleneck and require higher interconnect bandwidth without a proportional increase in electrical power consumption or the number of laser sources and fibre connections. Moving optical interfaces closer to computing chips reduces electrical transmission loss, while demanding optical engines that combine high channel capacity, broadband modulation and simple packaging. Although wavelength multiplexing relieves pressure on the fibre budget, integrating shared multi-wavelength sources with dense wavelength routing and broadband modulation in a compact format remains challenging. Here we demonstrate a monolithic transmitter that brings these functions together on a single material platform, enabled by the low birefringence and native Pockels response of thin-film lithium tantalate. The device separates, independently modulates and recombines eight wavelength channels between one optical input and output. This architecture retains a two-fibre interface as the channel count grows, directly addressing the packaging burden of parallel optical links. Measurements across the eight channels establish an aggregate line rate of 1.6 Tbit s$^{-1}$. Operation with a shared optical frequency comb achieves an estimated net data rate of 0.58 Tbit s$^{-1}$ across four channels, demonstrating compatibility with a common multi-wavelength source. Scaling this architecture into multiple wavelength-multiplexed engines offers a path towards 10 Tbit s$^{-1}$ optical interfaces with high bandwidth per unit package edge, positioning thin-film lithium tantalate for the next generation of co-packaged optical interconnects.

papers.title: Microcomb spectral fingerprinting enables parts-per-trillion methane detection with low humidity cross-sensitivity
papers.abstract: Optical frequency combs have transformed molecular spectroscopy by enabling broadband, high-resolution analysis, yet they are conventionally used as light sources to interrogate external samples. Here, we introduce an integrated microcomb sensing architecture that unifies resonantly enhanced evanescent sensing with multiwavelength molecular fingerprinting in a single ultrahigh-quality-factor silica microresonator. Gaseous analytes interact directly with the evanescent field of light recirculating within the resonator, enhancing sensitivity while encoding analyte-induced perturbations across the microcomb's collective spectral response. Rather than relying on a single optical resonance, we exploit distributed responses across multiple comb lines to generate multidimensional molecular fingerprints. Adding more comb lines systematically improves analyte discrimination, showing that the microcomb provides sensing information beyond what individual spectral channels offer. Using methane as a model analyte, we achieve an estimated detection limit of 178 parts per trillion, with minimal spectral responses to ammonia, carbon monoxide, hexane, and water vapor at relative humidities up to 90%. By replacing physically long interaction paths with resonant light recirculation in an ultrahigh-Q microresonator, this architecture brings compact optical sensing into the parts-per-trillion regime while exploiting distributed spectral information for chemical identification.

papers.title: Optical Response in Spintronic Poisson Bolometers
papers.abstract: Analog bolometers based on temperature-dependent phase-transition materials such as vanadium oxide (VOx) and barium titanate (BTO) represent the state of the art in uncooled infrared detectors. Recently, the first room-temperature spintronic Poisson bolometer based on magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) was proposed and demonstrated as a promising infrared detector. Unlike conventional bolometers, the spintronic Poisson bolometer operates in a probabilistic regime dominated by Poissonian noise, where the response is governed by resistance fluctuations arising from thermally activated magnetization transitions. Spontaneous transitions between two metastable magnetic states occur even in the absence of incident light, and the transition probability increases under illumination. In this work, we experimentally study the statistical properties of the optical response of the spintronic Poisson bolometer under illumination. We demonstrate that transitions in spintronic Poisson bolometers, both in the absence and presence of light, exhibit Poissonian behavior, with transition rates and interarrival times modulated by incident radiation. Under illumination, we observe a 153% increase in the count rate accompanied by a 70% reduction in interarrival time. These results establish spintronic Poisson bolometers as a promising platform for probabilistic, high-speed, and high-sensitivity infrared detection at room temperature.

papers.title: Edge-enhanced diffractive neural networks based on spin-multiplexed nonlocal metasurfaces
papers.abstract: Single-layer diffractive neural networks often face classification accuracy bottlenecks due to limited wavefront modulation capabilities. Edge detection, as an optical image processing technique, extracts image contours and offers a promising way to simplify classification tasks. However, integrating edge detection and DNN-based classification on a single chip remains a challenge. Here, we propose an integrated nonlocal meta-platform that sequentially achieves all-optical edge detection and classification via spin-multiplexing. By exploiting the dispersion properties of the nonlocal Huygens' metasurface, the co-polarized component in the output light performs momentum-space filtering for real-time edge detection. Subsequently, the cross-polarized component undergoes geometric phase modulation to execute image classification within the DNN. We couple quasi-bound states in the continuum and magnetic dipole resonances in crescent-shaped nanopillars, achieving a high polarization conversion efficiency of approximately $55\%$. This edge-enhanced DNN architecture significantly reduces data redundancy, elevating the classification accuracy of the single-layer network on the MNIST dataset from $64.2\%$ to $80.7\%$. Our work provides a compact, high-efficiency solution for integrated all-optical machine vision and intelligent photonic computing.

papers.title: Counterdiabatic Raman Atom Optics for Compact High-Sensitivity Gravimetry
papers.abstract: Large-momentum-transfer (LMT) atom interferometry provides a route toward enhanced inertial sensitivity in compact quantum sensors, but its scalability is limited by the accumulation of pulse-transfer errors across long Raman pulse sequences. We investigate theoretically the use of stimulated Raman shortcut-to-adiabatic passage (STIRSAP) for high-fidelity LMT atom optics in a Mach--Zehnder interferometer geometry. The counterdiabatic correction is encoded directly into the Raman pulse envelopes, eliminating the need for auxiliary microwave or radio-frequency control fields. Numerical simulations based on an effective Raman model show that $1~\mu\mathrm{s}$ STIRSAP pulses achieve single-pulse transfer fidelities of $F_\pi = 0.99902$ while maintaining negligible pulse-time overhead even at high momentum order. We analyze the resulting tradeoff between interferometric phase enhancement and compound contrast decay and identify an unconstrained shot-noise optimum near $n\approx270$. The analysis further shows that practical operation at extreme LMT order is constrained by wave-packet separation, vibration noise, Doppler detuning, and accumulated systematic effects rather than by pulse duration itself. These results establish superadiabatic Raman control as a promising approach for scalable high-fidelity atom optics and clarify the physical limitations governing compact high-order atom interferometers.

papers.title: Site-Selective Activation of Near-Infrared Emitters in hBN
papers.abstract: Near-infrared (NIR) emitters in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) have recently emerged as bright and spectrally stable light sources, but they have so far been found at locations set by the local defect environment rather than by design. Here we show that NIR emitters can be activated at predefined sites by combining single-shot femtosecond laser writing with annealing in an oxygen-rich environment. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of site-selective activation of NIR emitters in hBN. The written matrices are recovered in post-anneal photoluminescence maps, including in collection bands centred at 800 and 900 nm. Site-resolved spectra under 532, 635 and 785 nm excitation show narrow lines extending to 1 um; 83% of the spectra acquired at written sites under 785 nm excitation and 71% under 635 nm excitation contain at least one resolved peak above 810 nm. The integrated emission increases with writing-pulse energy over the range studied, and many sites host more than one emitter, which identifies lower writing energies as the route to single-emitter occupancy. Photon-correlation measurements on selected sites show antibunching, with a raw, uncorrected second-order correlation value g(2)(0) of 0.31 in a band centred at 850 nm. Spectral time series reveal bands that persist over the recorded intervals together with intermittent emission beyond 900 nm. Comparison with identically written, argon-annealed samples indicates that the annealing atmosphere controls the spectral range of the activated emitters, while the laser defines where they form.

papers.title: Effect of Physical Barriers on High-Harmonic Generation in Liquid-Phase
papers.abstract: High-harmonic generation (HHG) in liquid-phase systems presents fundamental differences from gas and solid phases, notably a reduction in the harmonic cutoff, its apparent independence from laser parameters, and the appearance of a second plateau. In this work, we introduce a one-dimensional quantum model that incorporates physical boundaries to simulate the effect of solvation shells in liquid water by means of a complex absorbing potential (CAP). By systematically varying the position, width, and strength of the CAP, we explore how these physical constraints influence the HHG spectrum. Our findings confirm that spatial confinement, specifically the physical truncation of electron trajectories, is the primary factor governing the cutoff in liquid-phase HHG. This confinement leads to a cutoff that is independent of laser intensity and wavelength, aligning with experimental observations and existing hypotheses proposed by Mondal et al. in 2023 and 2026. Furthermore, by implementing a semi-transparent CAP, we successfully reproduce the less intense second plateau observed in liquid-phase HHG. Time-frequency analysis confirms that this characteristic spectral feature is driven by partial wave-packet transmission through the solvation shells, which allows a surviving fraction of electrons to undergo longer continuum excursions. Our one-dimensional approach successfully isolates the fundamental role of physical boundaries in liquid-phase HHG, providing a clear and intuitive understanding of the underlying physics.

papers.title: Demonstration of continuous non-invasive monitoring of plant metabolism using mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Life is a rhythmic process driven by cellular and physiological mechanisms that allow plants to respond and adapt to their environment. In addition to natural fluctuations, plants are increasingly exposed to environmental stresses, mainly caused by climate change and anthropogenic pollution. Multiple approaches across different biological scales (gene, cell, metabolite, and physiology) have shed light on acclimation mechanisms but generally lack sufficient temporal resolution. Establishing a non-invasive and high-temporal-resolution monitoring method to measure plant activity across different conditions is therefore needed to fully assess how plant metabolism changes under stress. Here, we established a novel approach to perform continuous and non-invasive mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy on vascular plants, with the aim of identifying and monitoring the chemical composition of peripheral tissues, including sap, over periods ranging from a few minutes to several months. We describe an experimental setup, the physics underlying its operation, and present a multi-day acquisition. Compared with controls, data enabled to identify a diurnal pattern, with peaks of approximately equal duration, that recurred consistently over the experiment. Estimations of the impact of instrumental and environmental fluctuations indicate that the signal amplitude and trends cannot be explained by instrumental drifts. The experiment thus demonstrated the detection of a signal associated with plant physiological activity. While its origins remain to be clarified, this preliminary experiment demonstrates the feasibility of the measurements and provides a basis for future developments.

papers.title: Entanglement and photoelectron holography in dissociative photoionization: molecular quantum eraser
papers.abstract: In a double-slit experiment with a bipartite system, the visibility of interference fringes depends on the availability of which-way information. Here, we report a Bell-like state of photoelectron and residual ion in the multiphoton dissociative ionization of the D$_2$ molecule. Evidence for entanglement is provided by the correlated emission directions of photoelectron and ion, which is observed using a COLTRIMS reaction microscope. In the presence of this correlation, the holographic interference fringes contained in the photoelectron momentum distributions are suppressed, indicating the existence of which-way information. The interference pattern persists when a single ionic state is populated and thus no which-way information is available. The experimental observations and conclusions are supported by the numerical solution of the electronic-nuclear time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation. Our work demonstrates that coincidence spectroscopy of ions and electrons is a powerful method for studying fundamental concepts of quantum information science within the context of ultrafast light-matter interactions.

papers.title: Freeform gradient-index media reconstruction
papers.abstract: Reconstructing a gradient-index (GRIN) medium consists of determining a spatial refractive index distribution that produces a prescribed ray trajectory, an inverse problem in geometrical optics. Previous approaches have used geometrical symmetries and conserved ray quantities to address this inverse problem. Extending reconstruction to freeform media requires approaches that do not rely on these symmetries. Here, we present a three-dimensional point-wise method for reconstructing freeform GRIN media through the inverse application of local refraction. The method does not require geometrical symmetry, paraxial approximations, or prior knowledge of the iso-indicial surfaces, and is straightforward to implement. Reconstruction using two interface geometries demonstrates that different refractive index distributions can be obtained from the same prescribed trajectory function. The choice of interfaces thus provides an additional degree of freedom for optical design, subject to local refraction conditions and compatibility between overlapping reconstructed regions.

papers.title: Quantum-Correlation-Based Multi-Emitter Localization in Information-Limited Regimes via Learned Inference
papers.abstract: Quantum correlation measurements have emerged as a powerful tool for localizing multiple emitters with subwavelength separation. Multi-emitter localization consists of two distinct tasks: identifying the emitter count $N$ and estimating their positions $\left\{x^{i}\right\}$. Existing fit-and-select frameworks fit the measured intensity and autocorrelation data using several models corresponding to different values of $N$ and then select the best-supported model. This procedure lets errors from the multi-parameter optimization of emitter positions propagate into the choice of model, degrading performance under photon-limited and high-background conditions. We propose a method that directly infers the emitter count and positions from the multimodal data via learned inference. Learned inference improves both the emitter-counting accuracy and localization precision compared to the fit-and-select method. It achieves more than tenfold improvement in precision and requires up to five times fewer photons to achieve practically meaningful localization with the largest gains observed under low photon counts, strong background, narrowly spaced emitter configurations, and spatially truncated data. This photon-efficient quantum-assisted localization framework offers a promising route toward real-time biological imaging and single-particle tracking in densely labeled samples.

papers.title: Charge-Selective Displacement of Spatiotemporal Optical Vortices at a Spatially Uniform Time Boundary
papers.abstract: At a spatially uniform, in-plane-isotropic time boundary, the transverse displacement of a spatiotemporal optical vortex changes sign with its topological charge, despite a charge-independent conversion weight. Radial spectral filtering couples to the vortex phase while preserving identical converted spectral intensities for opposite charges. For a narrow scalar Gaussian spectrum, the displacement follows the logarithmic slope of the spectral weight and occurs with zero mean transverse momentum. In a finite pumped GaAs waveguide, unequal attenuation during extraction adds angular deflection. Independent Maxwell--Drude simulations test this extraction-induced response and give $\pm42$~mrad before detector filtering. Calculated centroid traces at multiple planes separate propagation-induced drift from position offsets.

papers.title: Realization of valley-controlled orbital angular momentum via inter-orbital coupling
papers.abstract: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) represents a fundamental degree of freedom (DoF) for understanding novel phenomena in solids and synthetic lattices. However, the generation and control of OAM in lattice systems remain challenging. Here, we experimentally observe valley-controlled OAM states in inversion-symmetry-broken photonic honeycomb lattices consisting of s- and higher-orbital sublattices. These OAM states manifest as chiral vortex arrays in real space. By selectively exciting s-orbital modes carrying no initial OAM at either the K or K' valley, we observe higher-orbital OAM modes generated via inter-orbital coupling in neighboring sites. Specifically, s-p orbital coupling generates OAM states with topological charge l=+1 or l=-1, while s-d orbital coupling yields higher-charge OAM states with l=+2 or l=-2. The sign of the topological charge is determined by the valley DoF, enabling deterministic control of vortex chirality across the entire array. Our theory further reveals that a local vortex-chirality symmetry enforces the valley-dependent selection of vortex chirality at the K and K' valleys, establishing a direct connection between the valley DoF and real-space vortex chirality. These results establish a versatile platform for engineering chiral vortex arrays via orbital physics and exploring orbital- and topology-mediated phenomena in photonic systems and beyond.

papers.title: Superradiant temporal transition radiation of a relativistic electron beam
papers.abstract: A charge in uniform motion carries a bound field that does not radiate. Transition radiation releases part of it at a boundary in space. We propose and analyze the case of radiation emission due to a boundary in time: a relativistic electron bunch passes through an aperture in a semiconductor (silicon) wafer, and while its bound field occupies the wafer, a femtosecond laser switches the semiconductor into an electron-hole plasma. The field is a valid solution of the old medium and not of the new one, so it is handed to the plasma as an initial condition for radiation emission at the plasma frequency. Because in temporal transition radiation (t-TR) the wavevector is conserved, and the frequency is not, the emission can appear in a spectral band that the bunch's own field does not populate. Every electron contributes in phase to the initial condition at the switching moment, so the emitted energy scales as $N^2$. We derive the field energy conversion at the temporal boundary and the resultant measurable amplitude and frequency line-shape of the radiation taking into consideration plasma carriers collisional loss. The simplified analytical model of the process and its scaling laws are confirmed by use of FDTD numerical computations for a reference case based on the parameters of an existing 6.5 MeV photoinjector accelerator. For this case we predict wideband t-TR radiation emission at THz frequencies, where the emission center frequency, near the plasma frequency, is selectable across an octave, set by the laser fluence, and the intensity is governed by the beam charge. The predicted radiative energy is detectable in a single shot. The experimental considerations for observing it are given in a Supplement.

papers.title: Design and synthesis of laser inscribed flexible Bragg gratings containing silicon oxynitride-doped silicon thin film for authentication applications with the insights from X-Ray Absorption Spectroscopy and Quantum Mechanical Calculations
papers.abstract: Silicon-on-insulator is mostly the main driving material system for the field of silicon photonics, including PICs, due to high index contrast and compatibility with current semiconductor manufacturing processes [1]. A recent example is silicon oxynitride-doped silicon [2] discovered recently by our group, offering to set a new position for the fields of silicon photonics with a precise control of refractive index from 2.1 to 2.5 together with the photosensitivity property at different wavelengths. In this study, we demonstrate that the synthesis of silicon oxynitride-doped silicon can be performed on a flexible substrate for the fabrication of Bragg gratings (BG) at low temperatures below 100 degrees Celsius that are emerging for advanced applications. Their use in preserving ultra-fast lasers inscribed micro-information has been demonstrated numerically and experimentally due to its multispectral reflection behaviour from the ultraviolet (UV) to the near-infrared (NIR) regions. The unique structural characteristics of silicon oxynitride-doped silicon were studied at the Si L, O K and N K edges using soft X-ray absorption studies. The quantum mechanical calculations provide the potential formation mechanism of SiON-doped Si, whereas the crystal structure prediction for bulk Si3N4-xOx was conducted using the particle swarm optimization method in combination with density functional theory (DFT).

papers.title: Multiplicative Noise in Nanolaser Amplification: From Discrete Emission Events to the Additive-Noise Limit
papers.abstract: Laser amplification kicks off with just a few photons in the cavity, a regime where standard additive Langevin noise cannot capture the real fluctuations. To understand how this amplification begins, we map out a single-mode photon-carrier model that links macroscopic lasers directly into nanolasers. Stationary rate equations reveal that stimulated emission takes over across a tight pump window. In nanolasers, however, spontaneous processes coexist across a much broader range. Because steady-state averages miss the individual events that lead to the macroscopic photon number, we frame the stochastic dynamics around the actual discrete transitions, deriving a state-dependent diffusion approximation. The destruction of an excited carrier concurrent with the generation of a photon creates a negative photon-carrier cross-correlation. This unavoidably leads to a correlated, multiplicative Gaussian-noise framework. We track the resulting discrete dynamics with an established, event-based Laser Markov Chain (LMC) which stochastically samples pump, relaxation, emission, and cavity-loss events keeping all physical quantities as non-negative integers. Comparing its predictions to those of our multiplicative model proves that the latter reproduces excellently well the statistical behavior of photons and carrier, as long as a continuous diffusion description holds. Once the emission drops into the few-photon regime, however, the discrete model becomes indispensable. On the other hand, at large photon counts relative fluctuations shrink to a level where the state-dependence of the diffusion matrix can be ignored, to leading order, thus returning to the classic Langevin description of the system's stochastic dynamics.

papers.title: All-Dielectric Tight-Binding Photonics via a Band-Gap Vacuum
papers.abstract: Tight-binding photonics bridges condensed-matter physics and optics, providing a powerful framework for engineering band structures and topological phases with light. For photons, however, the vacuum is gapless, so resonators in air carry radiative tails that produce spurious long-range couplings. Here we embed resonators in a photonic band-gap vacuum (BgV), a photonic crystal whose band gap plays for photons the role vacuum plays for bound electrons. The BgV localizes each resonance exponentially, so designed short-range couplings define the lattice Hamiltonian. We thereby experimentally realize a faithful Benalcazar-Bernevig-Hughes Hamiltonian in an all-dielectric photonic crystal, resolving corner resonances and their orbitals in microwave measurements. Unlike the vacuum surrounding electrons, the BgV is itself designable, controlling relative couplings and closed-loop interference through its band dispersion and Bloch modes. Full-wave calculations and extracted models show that uniformly modifying the BgV, with all resonators fixed, switches the quantized polarization of a two-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice and converts a zero-flux lattice into a $\pi$-flux one. We also numerically realize three-dimensional pyrochlore and hyperhoneycomb lattices with space groups $R\bar{3}m$ and $C2/c$, the latter a nodal-loop semimetal with topological drumhead surface states. These results establish the BgV as a designable vacuum for all-dielectric tight-binding photonics in two and three dimensions.

papers.title: Measuring the Quantum Phase of Multiphoton Systems
papers.abstract: The quantum phase of a multiparticle system has remained a long-standing mystery in quantum physics. The absence of a phase operator that faithfully represents this physical quantity has prevented the formulation of a meaningful uncertainty relation with particle number. Here, we resolve this problem by measuring, for the first time, the quantum phase of multiparticle systems containing up to fifteen particles. We achieve this through a new quantum state tomography scheme that combines homodyne interferometry with photon-number-resolving detection. This approach enables us to reconstruct complementary photon-number and phase representations and establish the corresponding number-phase uncertainty relation. Our measurements further provide access to the mutually unbiased basis of a multiparticle system, a fundamental resource for multiparticle quantum information processing. Furthermore, we report the spatially resolved characterization of the quantum phase. These results provide an operational framework for measuring quantum phase in multiparticle systems, with implications for fundamental quantum physics and scalable multiparticle quantum technologies.

papers.title: High-Efficiency Silicon-Lithium Niobate Grating Coupler enabled by Fully-Etched Subwavelength Structures
papers.abstract: A new approach of silicon-lithium niobate (Si-LN) grating couplers (GCs) with a fully-etched structure is proposed. The coupling strength is engineered through subwavelength structures, allowing improved directionality. The adjoint-based inverse design method is simultaneously adopted to achieve efficient coupling between photonic circuits and fibers. Considering the birefringence of LN, the proposed Si-LN GCs are optimized and fabricated for TE mode along the crystallographic Z and Y directions. The experimentally measured coupling efficiencies are -3.3 dB and -3.9 dB along the crystallographic Z and Y directions, respectively. The measured 3-dB bandwidths are broader than 54 nm and the back reflections can be suppressed down to -15 dB over 50 nm for both directions. The proposed Si-LN GCs are realized by only single-step Si etching, offering a practical solution for fast device prototyping in Si-LN photonic integrated circuits.

papers.title: LIDAR with Optically Amplified Thermal Light
papers.abstract: Thermal light exhibits intensity fluctuations or photon bunching that has been used as a source of entropy or temporally correlated light. However, its low spectral density limits its use in practical applications like LIDAR. One method of remedying this is optical amplification to boost its brightness. In this paper, we show that the normalized second order coherence function $g^{(2)}(\tau)$ of a thermal light source is preserved after amplification. We then use amplified thermal light to demonstrate a LIDAR raster scan of a building at 1.3 km with a depth resolution of 2 cm.

papers.title: Study of non-uniformity-induced structured spectrum in a tapered optical fiber through stimulated four-wave mixing
papers.abstract: Tapered optical fibers offer tunable dispersion and a small mode area, yielding high nonlinearity, which makes them ideal for nonlinear and quantum optics. Because phase-matched four-wave mixing strongly depends on dispersion, the taper diameter becomes a key parameter. For sub-micrometer tapers, identifying the exact diameter is challenging. Here, we show that when seeding with a broad spectrum, stimulated four-wave mixing yields a comb-like spectrum that is directly linked to the overall taper profile opening possibility for non-destructive evaluation of sub-micron taper. Our model based on joint-spectral amplitude includes the phase accumulated over the fiber length.
